Remarks (added by pf02, May 2026)[edit]

: The solution given above is wrong in two very important ways. First, it is incorrect, and second, it is incomplete.

: It is incorrect because it assumes that (and hence as well) are in a plane. This is not necessarily the case. It could happen that is not in the plane defined by (or equivalently, is not in the plane defined by ). This is used several times in the proof. For example, in the equalities following [Equation 1], the author uses . This is true only if are in the same plane. Later in the proof, the author says "Since points , and are on the plane perpendicular to the plane with points , and , then these points lie on the big circle of the sphere." This does not make sense. The author just wants to say that is a right triangle, with . Again, this is not true in general; it is true only when are co-planar.

This error can be fixed. I will show a little later an idea which could be used so that we could reduce the general situation to the case when are co-planar.

: The solution above is incomplete because showing that the locus is the sphere of radius means not only showing that any point constructed as the diagonal of the parallelepiped is on the sphere, but also showing that for any point on the sphere it is possible to find on the sphere, such that are pairwise perpendicular, and such that is the the diagonal of the parallelepiped. This second part turns out to be non-trivial. Below I will give another solution in which I will prove this part as well.

: Here is an idea for a possible way to correct the half-proof given in Solution 1. Note that a triad can be rotated around such that move on the sphere, and stay pairwise perpendicular. The line stays fixed, although the point could in principle move on the line. As we rotate the triad , there will be one position in which the plane goes through the point . In this case, the half-proof given above is correct. If we proved that the point stays fixed (or that or are independent of the rotation) then we could assume that are co-planar. I will not pursue this line of thought further.

: Here is an interesting observation. Consider the same problem in 2D: we are given a circle, inside, on the circle such that , and defined as the other end of diagonal of the rectangle formed by . (As hinted by Solution 1 above, the locus of is the circle of radius centered at ([Equation 6])).

Let us contemplate the degrees of freedom in the 2D problem. We have one degree of freedom (say, defined by the angle ). In principle, is uniquely determined (assume we go clockwise from to ), so is uniquely determined. So depends on one parameter, and as such we expect it to be on a curve (which happens to be a circle).

Now contemplate the degrees of freedom in the 3D problem. We have three degrees of freedom. Indeed, choosing introduces two parameters. Choosing such that introduces one more parameter. Now is uniquely determined (we just need to fix an orientation), and calculating is uniquely determined. So depends on three parameters. As such, we would expect the locus of to be a 3D object (a "volume"; we would expect it to be a surface if depended on two parameters).

However, as hinted in the previous remark, is probably independent of a rotation. Which means that with parameters properly chosen, is independent of one of them, hence is dependent only on two parameters, so we expect to be on a surface.

This hints to another observation: in the 2D case, the correspondence between the set of pairs of orthogonal rays and points on the circle of radius is one-to-one. In the 3D case the function associating a point on the sphere of radius to any triad of orthogonal rays is surjective, but not one-on-one.

: The original problem given at the 1978 IMO was

" is a given point inside a given sphere. Three mutually perpendicular rays from intersect the sphere at points , and ; denotes the vertex diagonally opposite to in the parallelepiped determined by , and . Find the locus of for all such triads of rays from ."

The problem stated on this page and the original problem from the IMO are just notational variants of each other.
